headline: The AI boom meets a new test: demand, rates, and Chinese competition
dek: A powerful semiconductor cycle is supporting South Korean exports, but investors are questioning whether AI spending can justify current valuations as Chinese chipmakers advance.
story_title: When AI demand collides with market reality
story_html:
1. United States 🇺🇸 The global AI trade is entering a more demanding phase. On October 13, investors sold semiconductor and technology shares as concerns grew that rising interest rates could make data-centre projects less profitable. The immediate issue is not necessarily a collapse in AI demand; rather, markets are reassessing how much future growth has already been priced into company valuations. Higher borrowing costs increase the expense of building large computing networks, while investors are becoming more selective about which firms can turn AI investment into reliable cash flow. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/brutal-session-for-chip-stocks-shows-ai-trade-is-turning-ce785ddddd8ff322?utm_source=openai))

2. China 🇨🇳 China is central to this reassessment because its chip industry is making visible progress. Reports of advances by memory-chip producer ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, intensified fears that Chinese companies could eventually compete more directly with South Korean and Japanese suppliers. That possibility matters beyond China: greater supply from a new competitor could put downward pressure on memory prices and reduce profit margins across the industry. At the same time, China’s progress reflects a broader policy effort to reduce dependence on foreign technology, especially in strategically important sectors. ([jp.investing.com](https://jp.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/article-1709290?utm_source=openai))

3. Japan 🇯🇵 Japan’s market felt the shock even though its industrial position differs from Korea’s. The Nikkei 225 fell sharply on October 13, with memory-chip maker Kioxia among the companies hit by the technology sell-off. Japanese firms are important suppliers of semiconductor equipment, materials, and components, so weaker expectations for chipmakers can affect the wider manufacturing chain. Meanwhile, the Bank of Japan reported that September producer prices were 6.8% higher than a year earlier, although they fell 0.3% from August. This combination suggests that Japanese companies are still facing substantial cost pressure even as markets debate the strength of technology demand. ([jp.investing.com](https://jp.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/article-1709290?utm_source=openai))

4. South Korea 🇰🇷 South Korea shows the strongest contrast between business fundamentals and market sentiment. Customs data showed that exports reached $26.1 billion during October 1–10, up 102% from a year earlier, while semiconductor exports reached a record for that period. The figures underline how strongly AI-related demand is supporting Korea’s external sector. Yet Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares were among the companies exposed to the sell-off, because investors fear that Chinese competition and higher financing costs could eventually weaken the cycle. The shared theme across these four economies is therefore not simply “AI is strong” or “AI is weak.” It is a transition from unquestioned optimism to a more selective contest over technology, pricing power, and returns on capital. ([customs.go.kr](https://www.customs.go.kr/kcs/na/ntt/selectNttInfo.do?bbsId=1362&mi=2891&nttSn=10179143&nttSnUrl=2fbd97b6ed3711c34f4810ce485a72ce))
b2_summary: AI-related demand is still supporting semiconductor exports, especially in South Korea. However, investors are becoming more cautious. Higher interest rates can make data-centre construction more expensive, while Chinese chipmakers are advancing and may increase competition. Japan’s technology shares fell, and its producer prices remained high. South Korean exports were exceptionally strong in early October, but its major chip companies also suffered heavy share-price declines. The main theme is a shift from broad optimism about AI to a more selective market focused on profits, prices, and investment returns.

concept.title: Pricing power
concept.explanation: Pricing power is a company’s ability to raise prices without losing many customers. A firm with strong technology or a limited number of competitors usually has more pricing power. If new competitors increase supply, pricing power can weaken and profit margins may fall.

quiz.question: Why can higher interest rates hurt the AI investment cycle?
options: They make data-centre and computing projects more expensive to finance.
They prevent Chinese companies from producing memory chips.
quiz.explanation: Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs, so companies may delay or reduce expensive AI infrastructure projects.

one_sentence: The AI boom is not disappearing; it is becoming a stricter test of who can convert enormous investment into durable profits.
